title: Devarim: the man of few words speaks (Deuteronomy 1:1)
hookLine: the one who said he was no man of words now speaks a whole book

lines: I AM NOT A MAN OF WORDS.
FORTY YEARS LATER: A WHOLE BOOK.
cards: Go back forty years, to a bush on fire in the desert. God tells a shepherd to go to Pharaoh, and the shepherd argues. In the old Jewish translation of Exodus he says, "I am not a man of words."
He's slow of speech, he says, slow of tongue. Send someone else. God sends his brother Aaron along to do the talking.
Now jump to the edge of the Jordan. The shepherd is an old man of a hundred and twenty. And the book that opens today is almost entirely him, talking, speech after speech.

teach.h: THE MAN WHO SAID HE HAD NONE.
teach.b: The book begins: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel." In Hebrew, eleh ha-devarim. Devarim means words.
The rabbis heard the irony right away. A midrash, in Deuteronomy Rabbah, sets the two verses side by side. At the bush, the Hebrew is lo ish devarim anochi, not a man of devarim.

teach.h: THE SAME WORD, FORTY YEARS APART.
teach.b: The same word, forty years apart. Before, he couldn't speak. Now he speaks a whole book.
What changed? The midrash's answer is that living with the Torah healed his tongue. Another way to hear it: forty years happened.

teach.h: TABLETS BROKEN, A SISTER AND BROTHER LOST.
teach.b: He led a people who complained, he lost his sister and his brother, he broke tablets and carved new ones. Someone who has carried that much has something to say, and maybe stops worrying whether it comes out beautifully.
And look at who he's speaking to: a generation that mostly wasn't there for the start of it, their parents having died in the wilderness.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS OUT LOUD.
teach.b: The man who once asked for someone else to do the talking is now the one who remembers out loud for everyone. He doesn't need to be polished. He needs to have been there.
So the book of words belongs to the man who once had none. They didn't come from talent. They came from time.

how: Jewish communities begin reading Deuteronomy in the synagogue each summer with the portion Devarim, which is always read on the Sabbath just before Tisha B'Av.

games.q: inside the book of words — tap the pairs.
p: not a man of words, at the bush

s: Moses once told God he wasn't good with words
at the burning bush: "I am not a man of words."
the bush and Deuteronomy's opening use different words for words
both use devarim: not a man of devarim, and these are the devarim.
a midrash says living with the Torah healed Moses' speech
Deuteronomy Rabbah reads the two verses together and says his tongue was healed.

games.q: you're Moses at the burning bush, told to go speak to Pharaoh. what do you say?
o: I'm not a man of words. send someone else.
only if you make me king.
games.why: he argues that he's slow of speech. forty years later he speaks a whole book: these are the words.

practice: Think of a place where you usually stay quiet: a meeting, a dinner table, a group chat. Let one thing you know or need form as a single plain sentence, not eloquent, just true.
Say it to yourself a few times, until it sounds like you.

wordCard.voice: Devarim. Words, or things spoken. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, from its opening line, these are the words.

orig.note: Hebrew: words. what Moses said he lacked at the bush (Exodus 4:10), and the first key word of Deuteronomy.

carryVoice: Your line: words come with time. Plain is fine; true is enough. Day four hundred eighty-two.
